reviewEvidence.transcriptCaveat: Browser transcript export unavailable. Official on-picture English captions sampled every 0.5 seconds throughout the 189-second video and read in full; minor OCR artefacts remain in raw text. Japanese audio has not been independently transcribed or continuously listened to.
reviewEvidence.visualReviewMethod: Full-duration six-second contact sheets inspected, including physical figure before/after, all body-region annotations and artwork gallery; not every-frame review.
reviewEvidence.resolutionNote: Research-only reference media; never a production source. Independent production footage still requires genuine FHD or higher.

centralQuestion: What adjustments turn a rigid standing figure into a convincing character pose?
thesis: Work through the body's orientation, lines, silhouette and weight distribution while judging the intended camera view. Manipulating a tangible figure is useful training, but the individual suggestions support visual judgment rather than guaranteeing a pose by formula.

claims: Handling and posing an articulated figure can train an animation designer's eye.
The desired style matters; the suggestions focus on striking, expressive poses rather than guaranteeing anatomical realism.
A physical reference lets the designer test both the pose and the viewing angle.
sections.observedVisuals: Monster Hunter Rise weapon poses, then grey articulated figures demonstrating kicks, sword poses and two-body action.
exampleRoles: Monster Hunter Rise connects the posing exercise to an expressive game character.
Tangible figures provide a manipulable reference for body relationships and camera angles.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Independently sourced actual-game pose first, followed by our own rights-cleared pose reference or licensed rig on the fixed grid. If using a digital rig instead of a photographed figure, identify it as our demonstration and retain the useful recommendation to practice with tangible figures.
sections.transitionToNext: Apply the observation method to one neutral standing pose so every adjustment has the same baseline.

claims: Even a well-made character model can appear uninteresting when simply stood upright.
Changing the pose can create a much stronger impression without replacing the model.
sections.observedVisuals: Pit figma neutral standing pose compared with a revised, angled stance.
exampleRoles: One unchanged figure isolates pose as the cause of the visible difference.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Same licensed mannequin, lighting, lens and grid; compare neutral pose against the target. Then return to the neutral pose for progressive changes.
sections.transitionToNext: Decompose that visible improvement from the overall body line down to the extremities.

sections.role: Asymmetry, facing direction and connected body lines
claims: Avoid mechanically mirrored left/right sides for this expressive standing pose.
Turn away from a perfectly frontal presentation.
Lower and angle the head rather than leaving it square to the body and camera.
Offset the torso, hips and legs instead of placing them on one rigid line; the flowing relation can form an S-curve.
sections.observedVisuals: Centre line through Pit; face close-up with horizontal/vertical guides; red line through torso, pelvis and legs plus rotational arrows.
additionalPrerequisites: Define silhouette and the S-curve using the actual outline/body line, not an unexplained idealised drawing.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Reveal one change at a time on the grid rig. Keep a ghost of the prior pose and a short body-line overlay; avoid simultaneous camera movement while comparing each change.
sections.transitionToNext: The body establishes a flow that costume details and shoulders can reinforce.

claims: Choose an angle that shows the scarf's flow.
Cloth can billow to support the pose; the physical figure's rigid skirt limits this demonstration.
Set the shoulders strongly and raise them where the figure permits.
sections.observedVisuals: Pit torso close-ups reveal scarf, fixed skirt and shoulder positioning.
sections.retainedTeaching: Preserve the distinction between a useful pose intention and a physical reference's limited articulation. Cloth flow is an expressive design choice here, not a claim that the toy is a cloth simulation.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Use only a licensed asset with appropriate cloth/scarf controls, or add our simple authored non-character prop. Show the intended flow while labeling authored pose versus simulated motion truthfully.
sections.transitionToNext: Shoulder direction sets up the arms, but their silhouette must remain readable.

claims: Give the two arms different angles.
Bend them with the silhouette in mind without placing them too far from the torso.
Angle the wrists slightly instead of extending the hands as rigid straight continuations of the forearms.
sections.observedVisuals: Arm/torso spacing marked with circles; wrist close-up and curved arrow show a slight bend.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Keep the same camera; demonstrate arm symmetry, bend, spacing and wrist adjustment in that order. Briefly flatten the silhouette to verify that the hand/arm remains distinguishable.
sections.transitionToNext: With the upper body settled, adjust where the pose appears to carry its weight.

claims: Shift the apparent weight away from an exactly centred stance.
Angle the feet slightly outward and vary their distance from the camera.
Give the wings a convincing three-dimensional presence.
sections.observedVisuals: Feet have different foreground depths, shown with baseline guides; wings change orientation between neutral and posed examples.
sections.retainedTeaching: The source discusses artistic weight distribution, not a measured centre-of-mass simulation. Do not show a fabricated COM reading.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Use the grid to show foot depth and weight-bearing side. If the selected rig has no wings, retain the appendage-volume teaching role with an appropriate licensed winged model or clearly explain the corresponding visible prop rather than silently omitting it.
sections.transitionToNext: These many local adjustments now return to the full-body impression.

claims: A stationary pose already contains many interacting choices.
No checklist guarantees that the result looks good; evaluate the combined visual impression.
Poses implying movement require further care.
A weak underlying pose remains a problem even when the final artwork is polished.
sections.observedVisuals: Full before/after Pit comparison followed by Smash Ultimate artwork including Mario, Link, Kirby, Samus, Yoshi and Fox.
exampleRoles: Finished promotional poses confirm that the underlying pose supports the polished image.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Return to the same full-body before/after and one independently obtained rights-cleared finished-game image or gameplay pose. Show unchanged material/lighting so polish cannot conceal the structural comparison.
sections.transitionToNext: The practical way to improve that judgment is repeated hands-on posing and inspection.

claims: Practice by manipulating a physical figure and looking at it from useful angles to develop an eye for posing.
sections.ownScreenProposal: End with the completed pose on the grid and the retained body-line/silhouette checks, inviting a small hands-on pose comparison rather than adding an unrelated animation chapter.
